title: Sources & Methodology
text:
This study examines the relationship between tourism, accommodation capacity, employment, and economic activity in the U.S. Virgin Islands from 2000 through 2025. It uses descriptive time-series analysis and cross-source comparisons to assess the scale and unevenness of the territory’s tourism recovery following Hurricanes Irma and Maria (2017) and the COVID-19 pandemic (2020).
The analysis combines visitor statistics, accommodation surveys, federal employment and economic data, business census snapshots, and National Park Service visitation records. These sources measure different aspects of the tourism economy and are not treated as interchangeable.
The study is descriptive. It identifies changes and divergences across indicators but does not estimate the independent causal effects of hurricanes, the pandemic, or federal recovery spending.

title: Sources & Methodology
text:
Data Acquisition and Preparation
Original source files are retained in data/raw/. Source metadata, including URLs, local paths, coverage, frequency, and known limitations, are maintained in src/acquisition.py. Processing and loading functions are maintained in src/cleaning.py; chart construction is centralized in src/charts.py.
Manually extracted hotel statistics from USVIBER reports are stored as separate annual source files and combined by src/hotel_extraction.py. The extraction process checks for duplicate years, merges available, occupied, and occupancy series by year, and calculates an independent occupancy rate:
\[
\text{Calculated occupancy} =
\frac{\text{Room nights occupied}}{\text{Room nights available}}
\times 100
\]
The calculated rate is retained alongside the published occupancy series rather than assumed to be equivalent to it.
Census data are assembled from the 2007, 2012, 2017, and 2022 Economic Census releases. Overlapping observations are deduplicated by year and industry. Where vintages overlap, the earlier vintage is retained in the employment analysis.

title: Sources & Methodology
text:
Tourism Arrivals
Visitor statistics are drawn primarily from USVIBER Annual Tourism Indicators. The analysis uses published annual totals for total visitors, air visitors, and cruise passengers. These measures are retained as reported rather than reconstructed from visitor-type components, which do not consistently sum to published totals.
Historical coverage combines report vintages. TOUR24 supplies 2000 and 2010–2024 observations; TOUR10 supplies 2001–2009, where the later publication does not provide a consistent historical series. The change in source vintage is documented because some historical values were revised. Accommodation-related series are retained separately where their historical coverage is consistent across publications.
The analysis does not use the overnight-tourist series. Air visitors and cruise passengers are treated as separate published arrival measures, not as proxies for overnight stays or total visitor spending. The World Bank’s 2020 international-arrivals observation is excluded as an implausible outlier during the pandemic-related shutdown of cruise tourism.
Visitor counts represent arrivals, not unique individuals. They do not measure length of stay, visitor-days, or economic contribution. Comparisons with accommodation, employment, and economic indicators therefore describe related dimensions of the tourism economy rather than a direct accounting relationship.

title: Sources & Methodology
text:
Employment and Compensation
Three sources provide complementary measures of employment:

FRED Leisure and Hospitality: Monthly seasonally adjusted and non-seasonally adjusted employment. Annual values are calculated as the mean of the twelve monthly observations, not their sum. The series covers the broader Leisure and Hospitality sector (NAICS 71 and 72), not tourism alone.
USVIBER tourism employment: Published employment categories for hotels and lodging, and eating and drinking establishments. The available series ends in 2022.
BLS Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW): Annual average employment, wages, and establishments for NAICS 72, 721, and 722. QCEW counts covered jobs rather than unique workers and excludes self-employed and other uncovered workers.

Census employment figures are March pay-period snapshots, not annual averages. Census, QCEW, FRED, and USVIBER employment figures are therefore compared as indicators of related activity, not as equivalent counts.
QCEW average annual pay is calculated as total annual wages divided by annual average employment. Nominal wages and payroll are adjusted to approximate 2016 dollars using the mainland U.S. CPI-U. This is an inflation proxy, not a USVI-specific price adjustment.

title: Sources & Methodology
text:
Accommodation Capacity and Utilization
Accommodation capacity is measured using two distinct sources:

USVIBER annual tourism indicators: Survey-based counts of hotels, hotel rooms, and condominium or other accommodation units.
Economic Census: Establishments and guestroom counts for payroll-filing accommodation businesses, primarily NAICS 7211.

These sources have different coverage. The USVIBER survey includes a broader range of accommodation providers; Census counts are limited to businesses meeting its reporting criteria. Their totals are not combined.
Historical Census guestroom counts require a crosswalk between table formats. The 2007 and 2012 figures use the A10 industry total; the 2017 and 2022 figures use NAPCS product code 7003825000. The 2017 count is a December 31 observation, after Hurricanes Irma and Maria, and is not a pre-hurricane capacity benchmark.
Occupancy is examined using both USVIBER annual indicators and monthly hotel statistics extracted from USVIBER hotel reports. Published occupancy, calculated room-night occupancy, and broader annual survey occupancy are retained as separate measures because their reporting populations and comparability have not been established as identical.
The ratio of annual overnight arrivals to listed rooms was explored as a contextual measure. It is not treated as occupancy or actual room utilization: it does not account for length of stay, room availability throughout the year, or differences in accommodation type.

title: Sources & Methodology
text:
Economic Output
Territorial GDP and industry value added are drawn from BEA tables:

Table 1.1: nominal GDP.
Table 1.2: real GDP in chained 2012 dollars.
Table 2.1: nominal industry value added.
Table 2.3: real industry value added in chained dollars.

Real-dollar comparisons use BEA’s chained-dollar measures. No additional CPI adjustment is applied.
Accommodation and food services (A&F) value added is used as an indicator of activity in a relevant part of the visitor economy, not as a measure of tourism GDP. It excludes tourism-related activity in industries such as transportation, retail, and recreation, while including purchases by residents.
A&F’s share of GDP is calculated as nominal A&F value added divided by nominal GDP. This is an approximate industry share, not a complete accounting of tourism’s contribution to the economy.
BEA industry-level data end in 2021; GDP totals extend through 2022.

title: Sources & Methodology
text:
Recovery Comparisons
To compare indicators measured in different units, selected series are indexed to 2016, the last full year before the 2017 hurricanes:
\[
\text{Index}_t =
\frac{\text{Value}_t}{\text{Value}_{2016}}
\times 100
\]
An index of 100 represents the 2016 level. Values above or below 100 indicate levels higher or lower than that baseline.
Each series is indexed independently. Series without a usable 2016 observation are excluded. Missing observations are retained as missing; they are not interpolated or treated as zero. The resulting indices facilitate comparisons of relative change, not absolute scale.
Occupancy rates are not indexed. Changes are expressed in percentage points relative to the 2016 rate, preserving the distinction between a change in a rate and a proportional change in an underlying quantity.
A separate COVID comparison uses 2019, the last pre-pandemic year, as its baseline. It examines visitor arrivals, air visitors, cruise passengers, hotel rooms, FRED employment, and VIIS visitation.
No composite recovery score is calculated. The analysis compares the trajectories of individual indicators because recovery in visitor volume, accommodation capacity, employment, compensation, and economic output need not proceed at the same rate.

title: Sources & Methodology
text:
National Park Visitation
National Park Service visitation data are drawn from the IRMA database for Virgin Islands National Park (VIIS) and Buck Island Reef National Monument (BUIS). Annual and monthly observations are retained separately.
NPS visitation represents estimated recreation visits, not unique visitors. VIIS estimates also involve changes in counting methods over time. The 2003–2021 and 2022–2025 estimates are treated as distinct methodological periods; 2026 observations are excluded from long-term comparisons because of a major change to traffic-counter-based estimation. Missing BUIS observations for 1999–2001 are not interpolated.

title: Sources & Methodology
text:
Data Quality and Limitations
Source discrepancies and known data-quality issues are documented in src/validation.py. The project maintains a structured data-quality log recording the issue, severity, treatment, and implications for interpretation.
Key decisions include:

Excluding the anomalous 2020 World Bank international-arrivals observation rather than treating it as valid.
Using published USVIBER visitor totals and categories directly rather than reconstructing totals from components that do not consistently reconcile.
Combining historical USVIBER tourism-indicator vintages where necessary, while documenting material differences between publications.
Retaining gaps in NPS and hotel reporting rather than interpolating missing years.
Treating 2025 hotel observations as partial where the source reporting period does not cover a full year.
Using FRED employment after the USVIBER employment series ends in 2022.
Treating mainland CPI-U as an approximate deflator for USVI wages, not a local cost-of-living measure.

The analysis is constrained by differences in source coverage, definitions, reporting frequency, and revision history. Indexed comparisons reduce differences in scale but do not eliminate these limitations. Conclusions are therefore based on converging or diverging indicators, not on any single series.

title: Sources & Methodology
text:
Reproducibility
The project separates acquisition, validation, cleaning, hotel extraction, and chart construction into modules under src/. Raw source files are retained separately from processed datasets. Processed hotel statistics are generated from the curated extraction files; the analysis loads the resulting annual dataset.
The analysis scripts and source registry document the inputs and transformations used to produce the figures and comparisons. Data-quality decisions are recorded in the validation log.

title: Exploratory Data Analysis
text: This companion to the main publication documents the full exploratory analysis. All charts are generated from the cleaned datasets in data/interim/. The complete analytical notebooks — including detailed tables, validation checks, and additional charts — are in the notebooks/ directory.

title: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Section 1 — Visitor Activity

Tourism returned. The visitor mix did not.
By 2024, total visitor arrivals had recovered to approximately 97% of their 2016 level. That near-return to the pre-hurricane benchmark conceals a substantial difference in how visitors arrive.
Air visitors reached approximately 109% of their 2016 level. Cruise passengers, by contrast, recovered to about 90%. The headline arrival total therefore suggests a tourism sector close to its former scale, but the composition of that traffic has changed.
These measures count arrivals, not visitor-days or economic contribution. They cannot tell us whether the territory has recovered its former volume of overnight stays or visitor spending. They do show that recovery has been uneven across the two principal arrival modes.
Figure 1. Visitor arrivals by mode, 2000–2024. Annual total arrivals, air visitors, and cruise passengers. The 2017 hurricanes and 2020 pandemic mark two distinct disruptions. Values are published USVIBER measures; component series are not reconstructed to force agreement with published totals.
Figure 2. Visitor arrivals relative to 2016. Total arrivals, air visitors, and cruise passengers indexed to 2016 = 100. The index makes the difference in recovery trajectories easier to compare without implying that the measures represent equivalent visitor experiences or economic value.

Park visitation tells a different story
Visitor arrivals are not the only measure of activity associated with the territory’s visitor economy. Virgin Islands National Park visitation provides a separate indicator of recreation activity on St. John.
By 2024, reported VIIS recreation visits were approximately 103% of the 2016 level; in 2025, they reached approximately 115%. This recovery contrasts with the weaker accommodation and employment measures.
Park visitation is not a count of unique visitors, and it cannot be directly compared with territory-wide arrivals. A person may generate multiple recreation visits, and park use can include residents as well as tourists. The series also crosses a change in estimation methodology: 2003–2021 estimates and 2022–2025 estimates should be interpreted as distinct measurement periods.
The contrast is nevertheless useful. Park recreation activity appears to have recovered more strongly than several measures of the wider tourism economy. Whether this reflects a shift in visitor behavior, a difference in the populations being measured, or the effects of the revised visitation methodology requires further investigation.

title: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Section 2 — Employment

Employment has not followed arrivals back
Leisure and Hospitality employment offers a broader view of the sector’s labor-market trajectory. The FRED series includes both Arts, Entertainment, and Recreation and Accommodation and Food Services; it is not a tourism-only measure.
The annual average of seasonally adjusted employment reached an index value of approximately 91 in 2024 and 84 in 2025, relative to 2016 = 100. The 2025 figure therefore indicates a renewed decline from 2024, even as visitor arrivals in 2024 approached their 2016 level.
This divergence is important, but the measures should not be read as a direct productivity calculation. Arrivals count visitors; employment counts jobs across a broader set of industries. Differences in seasonality, visitor mix, labor intensity, wages, and the structure of the local economy may all matter.
Other employment sources provide useful detail but are not directly interchangeable. USVIBER tourism employment ends in 2022. QCEW provides annual average employment in Accommodation and Food Services, while Census employment is a March snapshot. Their differences in coverage and reference periods limit direct comparison.
Figure 5. Leisure and Hospitality employment, 2000–2025. Monthly seasonally adjusted employment, with annual averages and major disruption markers. The annual series summarizes the monthly observations; it is not a sum of monthly employment.
Figure 6. Employment across source definitions. FRED Leisure and Hospitality, USVIBER tourism employment, and Census/QCEW Accommodation and Food Services measures. The purpose is to show the available evidence and differences in scope, not to construct a continuous combined employment series.
Figure 7. Accommodation and Food Services employment and compensation, 2000–2025. QCEW employment, average annual pay, and total wages, with nominal and inflation-adjusted measures where appropriate. Average annual pay is wages per covered job, not a measure of typical individual earnings.
Interpretive question: The divergence between visitor arrivals and employment merits further investigation. In particular, the Census comparison suggests a substantial change in accommodation employment between 2012 and 2022. Before attributing this to a change in the industry’s labor requirements, the underlying establishment coverage and classification differences need to be examined.

title: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Section 3 — Accommodation Capacity

More visitors, fewer rooms
The accommodation picture is less straightforward. By 2024, reported hotel-room inventory stood at approximately 82% of its 2016 level. The recovery in arrivals has therefore taken place alongside a smaller recorded room base.
Reported hotel occupancy reached 66.3% in 2024, up from 56.7% in 2016. That is an increase of 9.6 percentage points. Higher occupancy alongside a smaller room inventory is consistent with greater utilization of the remaining capacity. It does not, by itself, establish that the accommodation sector has returned to its former scale or profitability.
The distinction matters. A smaller inventory can produce higher occupancy even when the number of occupied rooms or room nights remains below its earlier level. Occupancy is a ratio, not a measure of total accommodation output.
The available hotel statistics also have gaps and differences in reporting. The published USVIBER annual occupancy indicator and occupancy calculated from reported occupied and available room nights are not consistently interchangeable. The analysis should identify which measure is used in each comparison.
Figure 3. Accommodation inventory, 2000–2024. Reported hotel rooms and other accommodation units, where available. USVIBER survey inventory and Census establishment-based counts are shown separately because they cover different populations. The 2017 Census guestroom count is a post-hurricane snapshot, not a pre-storm baseline.
Figure 4. Hotel occupancy and room-night utilization, 2000–2025. Available and occupied room nights, with calculated occupancy where both measures are available. The 2025 observation is partial-year and should not be compared with full-year results. Missing years remain missing.
Interpretive question: Is the higher occupancy rate evidence of a more efficiently utilized, smaller accommodation sector, or does it reflect the loss of capacity and a narrower reporting population? The available data establish the change in inventory and occupancy, but do not resolve its cause.

title: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Section 4 — Economic Context

Tourism is not the whole economy
The BEA data provide a broader economic context, but they do not offer a direct measure of tourism’s contribution. Accommodation and Food Services value added includes activity serving residents as well as visitors. Conversely, tourism-related activity in transportation, retail, recreation, and other industries is recorded elsewhere.
Real Accommodation and Food Services value added reached an index of approximately 87 in 2021, relative to 2016 = 100. Its share of nominal GDP also declined from approximately 13% in 2015 to around 6% in 2020. These figures suggest that the industry’s economic position weakened during the period, but they do not isolate tourism’s contribution or establish why the share changed.
The wider economy also experienced extraordinary federal disaster-recovery spending after the 2017 hurricanes. That spending is relevant context when interpreting GDP during a period when tourism was severely disrupted. It should not, however, be treated as a demonstrated explanation for the trajectory of GDP without a more direct examination of the timing and channels of expenditure.
Figure 8. USVI GDP, 2002–2022. Nominal GDP and real GDP in chained 2012 dollars. The two measures answer different questions: nominal output reflects current-dollar economic activity, while chained-dollar GDP adjusts for price changes.

title: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Section 5 — Recovery Comparisons

An uneven recovery
Taken together, the indicators do not describe a single recovery trajectory.

Arrivals: Total arrivals were close to their 2016 level by 2024, but air and cruise traffic followed different paths.
Accommodation: Reported room inventory remained below its 2016 level, while occupancy rose.
Employment: Leisure and Hospitality employment remained below its 2016 benchmark and declined between 2024 and 2025.
Economic output: Accommodation and Food Services value added remained below its 2016 level in the latest available industry data.
Park activity: VIIS recreation visits exceeded their 2016 level by 2024 and 2025.

The distinction between recovery in visitor volume and recovery in the institutions, capacity, and employment that serve visitors is central to interpreting these results. A return in arrivals does not necessarily mean a return to the same tourism economy.
The evidence points to a sector that has regained much of its visitor traffic, but not necessarily its former capacity or economic structure. The available data cannot yet establish whether this represents a durable change in the composition of tourism, a lingering consequence of the hurricanes and pandemic, or some combination of the two.

title: After the Storm
text:
In September 2017, Hurricanes Irma and Maria struck the U.S. Virgin Islands within two weeks of each other. The territory took a direct hit from two Category 5 storms, destroying hotel infrastructure, damaging or closing Virgin Islands National Park, and disrupting the economy that tourism had sustained for decades. Three years later, before recovery was complete, COVID-19 closed borders and halted cruise shipping.
This study draws on data spanning roughly 25 years across six primary sources to document how the USVI tourism economy has moved through those shocks — and what recovery looks like in 2024 and 2025. Source coverage varies: USVIBER provides annual data from 2000, with 2001–2009 from an earlier publication vintage and 2010–2024 from the current edition; FRED employment begins in 1990; BEA data run 2002–2021/2022.

title: After the Storm
text:
In September 2017, Hurricanes Irma and Maria struck the U.S. Virgin Islands within two weeks of each other. The territory took a direct hit from two Category 5 storms, destroying hotel infrastructure, damaging or closing Virgin Islands National Park, and disrupting the economy that tourism had sustained for decades. Three years later, before recovery was complete, COVID-19 closed borders and halted cruise shipping.
This study draws on data spanning roughly 25 years across six primary sources to document how the USVI tourism economy has moved through those shocks — and what recovery looks like in 2024 and 2025. Source coverage varies: USVIBER provides annual data from 2000, with 2001–2009 from an earlier publication vintage and 2010–2024 from the current edition; FRED employment begins in 1990; BEA data run 2002–2021/2022.

title: After the Storm
text:
The two shocks




                            
                                            


Figure 1: Air visitors (all USVI arrivals by air) versus cruise passengers. Total visitors shown as context. 2001–2009 from USVIBER 2010 publication.




The 2017 hurricane shock cut total arrivals to 76% of their 2016 level within the same calendar year — notable given that the storms struck in September, meaning the first eight months of 2017 were largely normal. By 2018, the decline deepened as the full damage to hotel inventory became apparent.
COVID-19 in 2020 produced a collapse of different character: cruise shipping stopped almost entirely (cruise passengers fell to 25% of their 2019 level), while overnight tourists declined less sharply (to about 32% of 2019). The territory’s isolation and the absence of large-group gatherings may have made it modestly attractive to small-party leisure travelers once borders reopened.

title: After the Storm
section: A recovery that isn’t what it looks like
text:
A recovery that isn’t what it looks like




                            
                                            


Figure 2: Recovery index, 2016 = 100. Air visitors and cruise passengers (thick solid lines) are the primary arrival-mode comparison. Overnight tourists and context indicators (thin lines, reduced opacity) are shown for reference.




As of 2024, the index looks deceptively healthy at the top line. Total arrivals sit at 97% of their 2016 baseline. But that recovery in total arrivals masks a stark difference in visitor value. USVIBER data for 2024 imply an average of approximately $2,350 per overnight tourist trip, compared with roughly $450 per cruise passenger stop and roughly $400 per air excursionist — both in nominal 2024 dollars. These are implied averages per arrival in their respective categories, not daily spending estimates.
Air visitors — USVIBER’s reported total of all arrivals by air — reached 109% of their 2016 level by 2024. Cruise passengers reached 90% of their 2016 level. These two arrival-mode series have followed divergent trajectories since 2017. Employment and accommodation capacity, measured in hotel rooms, tell a compatible story: the sector is operating at roughly 80–90% of its pre-storm scale, but on a visitor base that has not recovered.

title: After the Storm
text:
What the park shows
Virgin Islands National Park on St. John covers roughly 60 percent of the island’s land area. Its visitation has followed a markedly different trajectory than territory-wide overnight tourist arrivals, making the two series an interesting comparative indicator — though they measure different things and cannot be treated as equivalent.




                            
                                            


Figure 3: VIIS NP estimated recreation visits vs. overnight tourists, both indexed to 2016 = 100. The park recovered to its 2016 level by 2024; overnight tourist arrivals remain at roughly 57%. This divergence is an open question, not a resolved finding.




VIIS NP visitation reached 103% of its 2016 level in 2024 and 115% in 2025. Overnight tourists, by USVIBER’s count, remained at 57% of 2016. The divergence is substantial enough to warrant investigation. Possible explanations include: changes in how NPS counts day-use visitors, increased use of the park by short-term rental guests (not counted as hotel tourists), or different recovery trajectories across segments of the overnight market. This is an open analytical question, not a resolved finding.

title: After the Storm
text:
Accommodation capacity




                            
                                            


Figure 4: Hotel room inventory (USVIBER survey) and L&H employment (FRED seasonally adjusted annual average), both indexed to 2016. Neither has fully recovered; rooms remain more constrained than employment.




Hotel room inventory tracked by USVIBER’s annual survey stood at 82% of its 2016 level by 2024. The U.S. Census Economic Census (which counts only payroll-filing establishments) shows a more severe contraction: 2,039 rooms in 2022 versus a 2012 peak of 5,027 — a 59% decline. The Census and USVIBER series use different methodologies and should not be directly compared, but they agree on the direction: accommodation capacity has not recovered.
Leisure and Hospitality employment (FRED, seasonally adjusted) ran at 91% of its 2016 annual average in 2024 — closer to baseline than hotel rooms. This may reflect leaner staffing in surviving hotels, or expanded employment in the food and entertainment segment that comprises a large share of the L&H aggregate.

title: After the Storm
text:
What the broader economy shows
Aggregate GDP and tourism activity tell different stories about the post-hurricane economy. BEA data show that USVI real GDP remained relatively stable in 2017 and grew in 2018–2021, even as visitor arrivals and accommodation revenue remained severely depressed. BEA attributed some of this growth to government spending and private fixed investment, which likely reflect hurricane response and reconstruction activity. These patterns illustrate how economic production can recover through activity outside the visitor economy while tourism itself remains impaired. This analysis does not estimate the contribution of federal disaster assistance to GDP.




                            
                                            


Figure 5: Accommodation and food services as a share of USVI nominal GDP (BEA data, through 2021). A&F value added is not equivalent to tourism GDP: it includes resident consumption and excludes tourism-related retail, transportation, and recreation.




Accommodation and food services value added — the broadest BEA measure of the sector’s economic contribution — fell from 13% of GDP in 2015 to 11.5% in 2017, collapsed to 6% in 2020, and rebounded to 11% in 2021, the last year BEA data are available. The rebound to 11% is encouraging but still below the pre-hurricane trend, and the GDP denominator during 2018–2021 likely reflects activity beyond the visitor economy. The sector had not returned to its pre-hurricane GDP share by 2021.

title: After the Storm
text:
Unresolved questions
This analysis surfaces some questions that the data alone cannot resolve:
What does 66% occupancy on a smaller room base actually mean for the economy? High occupancy on reduced inventory may reflect healthy operating margins at surviving hotels while masking a smaller aggregate economic contribution. The Census 2022 data (1,650 accommodation employees vs. 3,876 in 2012) suggests the surviving hotel sector is operating at significantly reduced staffing levels.
The full exploratory analysis is in the Analysis companion. Data sources, variable definitions, and methodological choices are documented in the Data Dictionary and Methodology pages.

title: After the Storm
section: The uneven recovery of the U.S. Virgin Islands’ tourism economy, 2000–2025
text:
The uneven recovery of the U.S. Virgin Islands’ tourism economy, 2000–2025
Tourism is the U.S. Virgin Islands’ economic lifeblood. It is also unusually exposed to forces beyond its control: hurricanes, pandemics, shifting travel patterns, and the fortunes of a handful of major visitor markets.
The territory has weathered two extraordinary disruptions in less than a decade. Hurricanes Irma and Maria struck in 2017. COVID-19 brought another collapse in travel three years later. By 2024, visitor arrivals had nearly returned to their 2016 level.
That sounds like a recovery. Look a little closer, and the picture gets more complicated.

The visitors came back
Total visitor arrivals in 2024 were about 97% of their 2016 level. But the mix had changed. Air visitors had reached 109% of the earlier benchmark; cruise passengers were still at 90%.
The headline number conceals two different trajectories. And arrivals alone tell us little about how long visitors stay, how much they spend, or how widely that spending circulates through the local economy.


The infrastructure did not
Reported hotel-room inventory remained below its pre-hurricane level. By 2024, it stood at roughly 82% of the 2016 figure.
Occupancy, meanwhile, had risen from 56.7% to 66.3%. More rooms were occupied as a share of a smaller available inventory. That may indicate stronger utilization of the accommodation that remains, but it is not the same as restoring lost capacity.
The distinction is easy to miss: a destination can fill more of its rooms without having as many rooms to fill.


The workforce tells another story
Leisure and Hospitality employment has not kept pace with the return in arrivals. Its annual average stood at about 91% of the 2016 level in 2024, falling to 84% in 2025.
This is a broad employment measure, not a count of tourism workers alone. Still, its trajectory raises a question worth asking: what does a return in visitor volume mean when employment remains below its earlier level?
The available data show the divergence. They do not yet explain it.


Recovery depends on what you measure
Other indicators reinforce the uneven picture. Real Accommodation and Food Services value added reached about 87% of its 2016 level in 2021, the latest year available for that industry measure. Recreation visits to Virgin Islands National Park, by contrast, reached 103% of their 2016 level in 2024 and 115% in 2025.
These are not interchangeable measures. Park visits are not unique tourists; industry value added is not tourism GDP. But together they show why no single number can stand in for the health of the visitor economy.


A return, but not a reset
The U.S. Virgin Islands has recovered much of its visitor traffic. That is a significant achievement after two major shocks. But arrivals, accommodation capacity, employment, economic output, and park visitation tell different stories.
The evidence points to a tourism economy that has regained much of its volume without clearly restoring its former scale or structure. Whether this reflects a lasting change or an incomplete recovery remains an open question.
The distinction matters. Counting visitors tells us whether people are coming back. It does not, by itself, tell us what kind of economy they are coming back to.

title: Data Dictionary
text:
This study draws on tourism, employment, accommodation, economic, and national park records to examine change in the U.S. Virgin Islands from 2000 through 2025. Sources differ in coverage, frequency, definitions, and reporting practices; the measures are not always directly comparable.
Raw source files are stored in data/raw/. Source URLs, local file paths, coverage, and acquisition notes are catalogued in src/acquisition.py. Validation findings and documented data-quality decisions are maintained in src/validation.py.

title: Data Dictionary
text:
Sources and measures









Source
Data used
Coverage
Units and notes




USVI Bureau of Economic Research (USVIBER)
Visitor arrivals and expenditures; visitor types and modes; accommodation inventory; hotel occupancy; tourism employment
Varies by series; generally 2000–2025
Visitor counts, rooms/units, percentages, employment, and nominal dollars. Annual Tourism Indicator reports and historical statistical publications use different vintages and sometimes revise earlier values.


World Bank, World Development Indicators
International tourist arrivals and tourism receipts
1995–2020
Arrivals in persons; receipts in current US dollars. The reported 2020 arrivals figure (8.6 million) is anomalous and is treated as missing.


Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED) / Bureau of Labor Statistics
Monthly U.S. Virgin Islands Leisure and Hospitality employment; Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U)
Employment: 1990–2026; CPI-U: 1913–2026
Employment is reported in thousands of jobs, seasonally adjusted and not seasonally adjusted. Leisure and Hospitality covers NAICS 71 and 72; it is broader than tourism employment. Mainland CPI-U is used as an inflation proxy where real compensation measures are shown.


BLS Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW)
Accommodation and Food Services employment and wages; NAICS 72, 721, and 722
2000–2025
Annual average employment, total wages, and average annual pay. Covers jobs reported under the unemployment insurance system, not all workers or unique individuals.


U.S. Census Bureau, Economic Census
Establishments, employment, receipts, payroll, and guestroom counts
2007, 2012, 2017, 2022
Periodic economic snapshots, not annual series. Employment refers to the March pay period. Guestroom counts use different industry/product classifications across vintages.


Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA)
USVI GDP and Accommodation and Food Services value added
GDP: 2002–2022; industry value added: 2002–2021
GDP and industry value added in current dollars and chained 2012 dollars. Accommodation and Food Services is not a measure of tourism alone.


National Park Service, IRMA
Annual recreation visits to Virgin Islands National Park (VIIS) and Buck Island Reef National Monument (BUIS)
VIIS: 1957–2025; BUIS: 1962–2025
Estimated recreation visits, not unique visitors. BUIS has no observations for 1999–2001. VIIS estimates use different methodologies across the study period.


USVIBER hotel reports
Annual room nights available, room nights occupied, and reported occupancy
Varies by measure; generally 2000–2025
Compiled from annual hotel-statistics PDFs. The extracted series contains gaps and reporting inconsistencies; 2025 occupied nights and occupancy are partial-year observations and are excluded from full-year comparisons.

title: Data Dictionary
text:
Source-specific qualifications
Visitor statistics. USVIBER publications do not always report internally consistent totals. Published total visitors, excursionists, and air visitors are retained as separate measures rather than reconstructed from components that do not reliably sum to the published totals. Historical reports also revise some earlier years. The analysis uses a documented combination of report vintages; figures near the transition between vintages should be interpreted with care.
Accommodation data. USVIBER inventory surveys include a broader range of accommodation providers than Census payroll-based establishment counts. These are different measures, not competing estimates of an identical population. Census guestroom counts also require a classification crosswalk: the 2007 and 2012 figures use the A10 industry total, while the 2017 and 2022 figures use NAPCS product code 7003825000. The 2017 count is a December 31 snapshot, after Hurricanes Irma and Maria.
The hotel-report extraction contains 396 source observations from 66 PDFs. The selected annual series is retained separately from the source observations and conflict log. Available room nights begin in 2007; occupied room nights are missing for 2002; reported occupancy is missing for 2003 and 2018. The 2025 occupied-night and occupancy figures cover only part of the year.
Employment. The employment sources describe different populations and reference periods. FRED Leisure and Hospitality includes Arts, Entertainment, and Recreation as well as Accommodation and Food Services. QCEW covers UI-reported jobs in specified industries. Census employment is a March snapshot, while USVIBER tourism employment uses its own category definitions. These series provide context for one another but should not be treated as interchangeable.
Prices and compensation. Mainland CPI-U is used as a proxy to express QCEW wage measures in approximate 2016 dollars. It is not a USVI-specific cost-of-living measure. The available USVI CPI series ends in 2021 and contains a substantial 2018 discontinuity that has not been resolved; it is therefore not used as the deflator.
Economic output. BEA GDP and industry value added have different end years. Accommodation and Food Services value added includes activity beyond visitor spending and excludes tourism-related activity recorded in other industries. Its share of GDP is therefore an approximate measure of the industry’s contribution, not a tourism-GDP estimate.
National park visitation. VIIS visitation estimates from 2003–2021 and 2022–2025 were produced under different counting methods. The later series is treated as a distinct methodological period. Data from 2026 are excluded because the park shifted to a different traffic-counter-based approach. Park visits should not be interpreted as a count of individual visitors.

title: Data Dictionary
text:
Data availability and reproducibility
The project preserves source files separately from derived datasets. Acquisition metadata are recorded in src/acquisition.py; data loading and preparation are handled in src/cleaning.py. Hotel-report observations, selected values, and conflicts are retained in separate extraction outputs so that the annual series can be traced back to the underlying reports.
Missing observations are not interpolated. Partial-year figures, changes in source definitions, and unresolved discrepancies are identified rather than silently treated as continuous annual measurements.
